VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The notebook's data-preparation code re-samples (oversamples) training examples by drawing from the original full dataframe (df) after the initial train/validation split, then concatenates the new training set with the validation set and builds the FastAI DataBunch by index. This allows the same image rows to appear in both training and validation sets (i.e. leakage between train and val). Additionally there is an off-by-one in the index split that includes the last training-row index in the validation index range. Both issues mean the validation set is not a clean hold-out used for honest model selection.

EVIDENCE:
- Oversampling function definition: [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling.ipynb:230-231]
  "def balance_data(class_size,df):\n    train_df = df.groupby(['level']).apply(lambda x: x.sample(class_size, replace = True)).reset_index(drop = True)\n    ..."

- Initial balanced split into train and validation (shows they create train_df and val_df): [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling.ipynb:246-251]
  "balanced_df = balance_data(...)\n train_df, val_df = train_test_split(balanced_df,test_size=0.2)"

- Re-creating/oversampling the training set by sampling from the original full dataframe (this is the problematic line): [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling.ipynb:301-306]
  "train_df = balance_data(train_df.pivot_table(index='level', aggfunc=len).max().max(),df) # I will oversample ..."
  Note: the second argument passed is 'df' (the original full dataframe), not the previously-split train_df. This allows images that are in val_df to be sampled into train_df.

- Concatenation of the (new) train_df and val_df to create final dataframe and later splitting by index: [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling.ipynb:319-346]
  "df = pd.concat([train_df,val_df]) #beginning of this dataframe is the oversampled training set, end is the validation set" (line 320)
  "... .split_by_idx(range(len(train_df)-1,len(df))) ..." (lines 343-346)

- The split_by_idx call uses range(len(train_df)-1, len(df)) which includes index len(train_df)-1 (the last training index) in the validation index list (off-by-one). See both usage sites: [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling.ipynb:340-346] and [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling.ipynb:396-401].

Consequence / how this violates the test: because training examples are sampled from the full original dataframe and then later concatenated with the validation split (which itself was sampled earlier), identical images can appear in both the training and validation sets. This is data leakage between train and val: any model selection or hyperparameter tuning that uses that validation set will be optimistically biased. That fails the requirement that hold-out sets be free of leakage from training data.

If you want, I can produce a small proof script (and run it) that loads the CSV present in the notebook, replicates the same sequence of operations and demonstrates the intersection (duplicate file paths) between train and validation indices as concrete runtime evidence. To run that I will need the dataset files (or at least the trainLabels.csv referenced by the notebook) to be present under the same path the notebook expects (the notebook points to /kaggle/working/dataset).

EVIDENCE: 
- Oversampling function and its use before split: [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/nb_script.py:44-53] shows the balance_data function and the call that creates balanced_df from the full dataframe. Specifically lines 51-53:
  - 51: from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
  - 52: balanced_df = balance_data(df.pivot_table(index='level', aggfunc=len).max().max(), df)
  - 53: train_df, val_df = train_test_split(balanced_df,test_size=0.2)
  This creates a balanced_df (oversampled) and then splits it into train_df and val_df — i.e. oversampling was applied before splitting, so validation data is sampled from the already-balanced dataset.

- Code that later concatenates training and validation and builds the DataBunch: [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/nb_script.py:60-75, 89-96]
  - 60-63: shows a second call that reassigns train_df and then concatenates df = pd.concat([train_df,val_df]) with the comment that the beginning is oversampled training and the end is validation. However, because val_df was already sampled from balanced_df earlier, the validation set remains affected by earlier balancing. Lines 71-74 and 89-92 show the same split_by_idx being used on the concatenated dataframe to form train/validation sets in the fastai DataBunch.

- No evidence of weighted loss or sampler usage: repository grep results saved as artifact [/evidence/artifacts/grep_results.txt] show no occurrences of common imbalance-handling constructs (WeightedRandomSampler, class_weight, pos_weight, WeightedSampler, WeightedLoss). This indicates the imbalance handling is done via pandas oversampling rather than a training-only sampler or loss weighting. File: /evidence/artifacts/grep_results.txt

Conclusion: Because the code constructs balanced_df from the full dataset and then splits into train/val, class-imbalance handling (oversampling) is applied to data that becomes validation data as well. Therefore the test "Any class-imbalance handling (weighted loss / sampler) applies only to training data" FAILs for this repository.

metadata.reason_text: The repository performs class-imbalance handling (oversampling) before creating the train/validation split, which means the balancing affects the validation set as well. There is no evidence of loss weighting or a sampler being applied only to training.
metadata.evidence_text:
- Oversampling function and its use before split: [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/nb_script.py:44-53] shows the balance_data function and the call that creates balanced_df from the full dataframe. Specifically lines 51-53:
  - 51: from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
  - 52: balanced_df = balance_data(df.pivot_table(index='level', aggfunc=len).max().max(), df)
  - 53: train_df, val_df = train_test_split(balanced_df,test_size=0.2)
  This creates a balanced_df (oversampled) and then splits it into train_df and val_df — i.e. oversampling was applied before splitting, so validation data is sampled from the already-balanced dataset.

- Code that later concatenates training and validation and builds the DataBunch: [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/nb_script.py:60-75, 89-96]
  - 60-63: shows a second call that reassigns train_df and then concatenates df = pd.concat([train_df,val_df]) with the comment that the beginning is oversampled training and the end is validation. However, because val_df was already sampled from balanced_df earlier, the validation set remains affected by earlier balancing. Lines 71-74 and 89-92 show the same split_by_idx being used on the concatenated dataframe to form train/validation sets in the fastai DataBunch.

- No evidence of weighted loss or sampler usage: repository grep results saved as artifact [/evidence/artifacts/grep_results.txt] show no occurrences of common imbalance-handling constructs (WeightedRandomSampler, class_weight, pos_weight, WeightedSampler, WeightedLoss). This indicates the imbalance handling is done via pandas oversampling rather than a training-only sampler or loss weighting. File: /evidence/artifacts/grep_results.txt

Conclusion: Because the code constructs balanced_df from the full dataset and then splits into train/val, class-imbalance handling (oversampling) is applied to data that becomes validation data as well. Therefore the test "Any class-imbalance handling (weighted loss / sampler) applies only to training data" FAILs for this repository.

REASON: The notebook computes reported metrics (fastai accuracy and a quadratic Cohen's kappa) using the validation dataset defined in the notebook, but the split-by-index call that defines the validation indices is off-by-one: .split_by_idx(range(len(train_df)-1, len(df))). This includes the last training example in the validation set (the range should start at len(train_df)). Thus the metrics reported as being on the 80/20 validation split are not computed on the exact split the author described.
EVIDENCE: 
- The dataset split is created with sklearn train_test_split and the author comments that an 80%/20% split is intended: [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling.ipynb:249-251]
  - File excerpt: "train_df, val_df = train_test_split(balanced_df,test_size=0.2) # Here we will perform an 80%/20% split of the dataset, with stratification to keep similar distribution in validation set"

- The full dataframe df is constructed by concatenating oversampled train_df and val_df (train first, val second): [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling.ipynb:319-321]
  - File excerpt: "df = pd.concat([train_df,val_df]) #beginning of this dataframe is the oversampled training set, end is the validation set"

- The validation indices are supplied to fastai via split_by_idx using range(len(train_df)-1, len(df)), which includes the index len(train_df)-1 (the last example from the training block) in the validation set (off-by-one): [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling.ipynb:338-347]
  - File excerpt: ".split_by_idx(range(len(train_df)-1,len(df))) #Splitting the dataset"
  - Correct/expected behavior: the validation indices should begin at len(train_df) (not len(train_df)-1) so that all indices >= len(train_df) correspond to the val_df rows only.

- The metrics used to report performance are created and evaluated on the fastai Learner (fastai's accuracy and a custom quadratic kappa that uses argmax/top-1 predictions):
  - The learner is created with metrics=[accuracy] and validate() is later called (so fastai computes metrics on data.valid_dl): [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling.ipynb:439-445]
    - "rand_learn = create_cnn(data, models.resnet50, metrics=[accuracy])" and "rand_acc = rand_learn.validate()[1]"
  - The main learner uses accuracy and quadratic_kappa: [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling.ipynb:521-522]
    - "learn = create_cnn(data, models.resnet50, metrics = [accuracy,quadratic_kappa])"
  - The quadratic_kappa implementation is a wrapper around scikit-learn's cohen_kappa_score applied to torch.argmax(y_hat,1), i.e. top-1 predicted class: [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling.ipynb:484-487]
    - "return torch.tensor(cohen_kappa_score(torch.argmax(y_hat,1), y, weights='quadratic'),device='cuda:0')"

Because of the off-by-one in split_by_idx, the reported validation metrics are not computed on the exact 80/20 split the notebook claims. The metric definitions themselves (fastai accuracy = top-1 accuracy; quadratic_kappa uses argmax/top-1) match the notebook's descriptions, but the split mismatch causes the test to FAIL.

Executing the notebook to produce runtime logs would require the dataset and a working notebook environment; the off-by-one is visible statically in the code and is sufficient evidence for the failure.

  - File excerpt: "df = pd.concat([train_df,val_df]) #beginning of this dataframe is the oversampled training set, end is the validation set"

- The validation indices are supplied to fastai via split_by_idx using range(len(train_df)-1, len(df)), which includes the index len(train_df)-1 (the last example from the training block) in the validation set (off-by-one): [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling.ipynb:338-347]
  - File excerpt: ".split_by_idx(range(len(train_df)-1,len(df))) #Splitting the dataset"

  This is simple I/O (printing filenames). It is not a numerical elementwise operation that would benefit from matrix ops.

- Path construction (list comprehension over labels -> string ops): [/evidence/artifacts/notebook_code.py:40-46] contains:
    df['path'] = [os.path.join(base_image_dir, f'{x}.jpeg') for x in df['image']]
  This is string/path construction. It can be vectorized using pandas string operations (e.g. df['path'] = base_image_dir + '/' + df['image'].astype(str) + '.jpeg') but that is a string-vectorization, not a matrix algebra replacement; the current use is acceptable. - GroupBy + sampling uses pandas high-level API (no manual elementwise loop): [/evidence/artifacts/notebook_code.py:54-60] contains balance_data which uses df.groupby(...).apply(lambda x: x.sample(...)). This uses pandas' vectorized/grouped sampling and is not a manual element-wise Python loop that should be replaced by matrix ops.

- Callback control flow (per-batch label shuffling): [/evidence/artifacts/notebook_code.py:141-147] contains:
    def on_batch_begin(self, last_target, train, **kwargs):
        if train:
            idx = torch.randperm(len(last_target))
            return {'last_target': last_target[idx]}
  This uses PyTorch tensor operations (torch.randperm and advanced indexing) for shuffling — already vectorized on tensors; no Python-level elementwise loop.

    for name, param in learn.model.named_parameters():

- GroupBy + sampling uses pandas high-level API (no manual elementwise loop): [/evidence/artifacts/notebook_code.py:54-60] contains balance_data which uses df.groupby(...).apply(lambda x: x.sample(...)). This uses pandas' vectorized/grouped sampling and is not a manual element-wise Python loop that should be replaced by matrix ops.

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The training loop leaks validation data into the training set. Inside the cross-validation loop the code concatenates val_df back into train_df (so training includes validation samples), and then evaluates the model twice on the training set (result_test = attention_model.evaluate(x_train) instead of evaluating on the held-out validation generator). This means validation is not held-out for model selection/hyperparameter checks.
EVIDENCE: The problematic code was extracted from the notebook and saved to /evidence/artifacts/extracted_notebook.py. Key excerpts:
- The cross-validation split then re-adds the validation fold into the training set: [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_notebook.py:241-246] (shows "train_df, val_df = df.iloc[train_index], df.iloc[val_index]" followed immediately by "train_df = pd.concat([train_df, val_df]).reset_index(drop=True)").
- The training call uses validation_data, but the post-training evaluation incorrectly evaluates on the training generator twice: [/evidence/artifacts/extracted_notebook.py:276-284] (shows fit(..., validation_data=x_test, ...) then "result_train = attention_model.evaluate(x_train)" and "result_test = attention_model.evaluate(x_train)").
These lines provide direct, verifiable evidence of data leakage from validation into training and incorrect evaluation (which would also compromise model selection).

If you want, I can create a minimal patch that fixes these two issues (remove the concat so train and val remain disjoint; change result_test to evaluate on x_test), run the notebook or a small dry-run to demonstrate the corrected behavior, and save the diff. Let me know if you'd like that.

VERDICT: INCONCLUSIVE
REASON: The repository contains a Keras/TensorFlow training notebook that does log loss/history, but it cannot be used to determine whether training loss "generally decreases and plateaus" because (1) the training in the notebook is configured for only 1 epoch (so no multi-epoch loss trend can be observed), (2) the data-loading function purposely replaces decoded images with zeros (so training would not be meaningful), and (3) TensorFlow is not installed in the execution environment and the notebook expects Kaggle-style input files under ../input which are not present here. Without installing TensorFlow and providing the dataset (or running the notebook after changing epochs and fixing the image-loading bug), it is impossible to obtain runtime evidence of decreasing/plateauing loss.

EVIDENCE:
- The notebook converted to script shows the image parsing function that discards the decoded image and replaces it with zeros: [/workspace/repo/evidence_notebook_script.py.py:93-100]
    93	def parse_image(filename, label):
    94	    image = tf.io.read_file(filename)
    95	    image = tf.image.decode_jpeg(image, channels=3)
    96	    image = tf.image.resize(image, [224, 224])
    97	    image = tf.zeros([224, 224, 3], dtype=tf.float32)
    98	    image = image / 255.0
    99	    return image, label

- The training loop calls model.fit with epochs=1 (so no multi-epoch loss curve is generated): [/workspace/repo/evidence_notebook_script.py.py:365-366]
    365	# Train the model
    366	history = attention_model.fit(x_train, steps_per_epoch=x_train.samples // 32, epochs=1, validation_data=x_test, validation_steps=x_test.samples // 32, callbacks=callbacks)

- The code does collect history items (history.history['loss'] etc.) and later plots mean_history['loss'], but because epochs=1 per fold this does not permit observing a decreasing/plateauing curve: [/workspace/repo/evidence_notebook_script.py.py:382-387] and [/workspace/repo/evidence_notebook_script.py.py:426-444]
    382	all_history['categorical_accuracy'].append(history.history['categorical_accuracy'])
    383	all_history['val_categorical_accuracy'].append(history.history['val_categorical_accuracy'])
    384	all_history['loss'].append(history.history['loss'])
    385	all_history['val_loss'].append(history.history['val_loss'])
    386	all_history['auc'].append(history.history['auc'])
    387	all_history['val_auc'].append(history.history['val_auc'])

    426	mean_history = {key: np.mean(np.array(all_history[key]), axis=0) for key in all_history.keys()}
    437	plt.subplot(1, 3, 2)
    438	plt.plot(mean_history['loss'], label='Train Loss')
    439	plt.plot(mean_history['val_loss'], label='Test Loss')

- Environment check showing TensorFlow is not installed (written to /evidence/artifacts/env_check.txt): [/evidence/artifacts/env_check.txt:1-3]
    python 3.11.13 | packaged by conda-forge | (main, Jun  4 2025, 14:48:23) [GCC 13.3.0]
    tensorflow IMPORT_ERROR No module named 'tensorflow'
    torch 2.8.0+cu129

WHAT IS NEEDED TO MAKE A CONCLUSIVE DETERMINATION (exact steps you can run locally or in CI):
1) Install TensorFlow (the notebook uses tf.keras and TF data pipelines). Example: pip install "tensorflow>=2.10" (match GPU/CPU availability). 2) Provide the image dataset expected by the notebook under ../input/diabetic-retinopathy-detection/ (or adapt the code to point to local data). The notebook currently expects to unzip ../input/diabetic-retinopathy-detection/trainLabels.csv.zip and parts of train.zip. 3) Fix the image parsing function so it uses the decoded & resized image instead of replacing it with zeros (change line 97 to remove the tf.zeros assignment). Concretely, modify parse_image to return the resized/normalized decoded image.
   - Suggested change at [/workspace/repo/evidence_notebook_script.py.py:96-99]: replace lines 96-98 with:
       image = tf.image.resize(image, [224, 224])
       image = image / 255.0
4) Increase epochs to a value > 1 (e.g., epochs=10) in the attention_model.fit call so loss over epochs can be observed (modify line 366 to epochs=10). 5) Re-run the notebook / script and capture the history object and loss per epoch (save to a CSV in /evidence/artifacts/training_history.csv and a plot /evidence/artifacts/loss_curve.png). Example code to save history after training:
       import pandas as pd
       pd.DataFrame(history.history).to_csv('/evidence/artifacts/fold1_history.csv', index=False)

If those steps are executed and you provide the produced training_history CSVs or plots, I can re-evaluate and give a PASS/FAIL with direct runtime evidence (loss values per epoch showing a decreasing trend and plateau).

Note: There is also a logical issue where the notebook sets attention_model.trainable = False after creating the model (line 355), which freezes the whole model and would prevent learning unless intentional — this should be reviewed. The combination of frozen pretrained layers, zeroed images, and epochs=1 means the current notebook as-is cannot demonstrate the requested property.

Summary: I cannot conclude PASS or FAIL from the repository alone because the code is not runnable in this environment (missing TensorFlow and dataset) and the notebook is configured such that it would not yield a multi-epoch loss curve (epochs=1 and image bug). Provide the environment + data or run the exact modification steps above and attach the resulting logs and I'll re-run the check.

   - File: [/workspace/repo/cnn-based-detection-of-diabetic-retinopathy/cnn-based-detection-of-diabetic-retinopathy.py:197-205]
     - Code excerpt (lines 199-201):
       trainLabels['path'] = [os.path.join(base_image_dir, '{}.jpeg'.format(x)) for x in trainLabels['image']]
       trainLabels['exists'] = [os.path.exists(p) for p in trainLabels['path']]  # Filter out missing images
     - Why this is improvable: constructing a pandas Series of file paths can be done with vectorized string operations which are implemented in C and faster than Python-level list comprehensions.
     - Suggested vectorized replacement (exact same result):
       trainLabels['path'] = base_image_dir + '/' + trainLabels['image'].astype(str) + '.jpeg'
       # There is no fully vectorized os.path.exists in pandas, but you can still avoid a python list comprehension by using Series.map (which is clearer):
       trainLabels['exists'] = trainLabels['path'].map(lambda p: os.path.exists(p))
       # If you prefer a pure numpy approach (may be faster for many entries):
       import numpy as np
       exists_arr = np.fromiter((os.path.exists(p) for p in trainLabels['path']), dtype=bool, count=len(trainLabels))
       trainLabels['exists'] = exists_arr
     - Note: the first line replacement uses pandas vectorized string concatenation; the exists check must ultimately call OS per-path, but using Series.map or numpy.fromiter is clearer and avoids creating an intermediate Python list.

2) Streaming nested loops over tf.data Dataset to pick one example per class (can be implemented via array/mask ops after materializing batches)
   - File: [/workspace/repo/cnn-based-detection-of-diabetic-retinopathy/cnn-based-detection-of-diabetic-retinopathy.py:164-179]
     - Code excerpt (lines 165-178):
       def get_images_by_label(dataset, num_classes=5):
           images = [None] * num_classes
           labels = [None] * num_classes
           label_counts = {i: 0 for i in range(num_classes)}

           for image_batch, label_batch in dataset:
               for img, lbl in zip(image_batch, label_batch):
                   label = int(lbl)
                   if label_counts[label] == 0:
                       images[label] = img
                       labels[label] = lbl
                       label_counts[label] += 1
                   if sum(label_counts.values()) == num_classes:
                       return np.array(images), np.array(labels)
           return np.array(images), np.array(labels)
     - Why this is improvable: the nested Python loops iterate per-sample while the same outcome (one sample per class) can be produced by materializing the dataset into arrays and then using numpy boolean indexing/argmax to pick first occurrences per class. That replacement moves the per-sample work into vectorized numpy operations.
     - Suggested vectorized approach (conceptual replacement):
       # materialize dataset into arrays (one-time loop to collect batches, unavoidable when using tf.data)
       imgs = []
       lbls = []
       for image_batch, label_batch in dataset:
           imgs.append(image_batch.numpy())
           lbls.append(label_batch.numpy())
       imgs = np.concatenate(imgs, axis=0)
       lbls = np.concatenate(lbls, axis=0)

       # vectorized selection of first instance per class
       images_out = np.empty((num_classes,)+imgs.shape[1:], dtype=imgs.dtype)
       labels_out = np.empty((num_classes,), dtype=lbls.dtype)
       for c in range(num_classes):
           mask = (lbls == c)
           idx = np.argmax(mask)  # returns first True; ensure class exists
           images_out[c] = imgs[idx]
           labels_out[c] = lbls[idx]
       # Note: the final small loop over classes (num_classes typically small) is negligible compared to per-sample loops.
     - Explanation: the initial collection of all batches must iterate once over dataset; after that, the heavy, per-sample selection is performed by numpy masks and argmax/boolean indexing (vectorized), avoiding nested per-sample Python loops.

3) Confusion-matrix text annotation uses double loop over matrix entries (visualization; can be vectorized but not performance-critical)
   - File: [/workspace/repo/cnn-based-detection-of-diabetic-retinopathy/cnn-based-detection-of-diabetic-retinopathy.py:467-476]
     - Code excerpt (lines 475-476):
       for i, j in itertools.product(range(average_cm.shape[0]), range(average_cm.shape[1])):
           plt.text(j, i, format(average_cm[i, j], '.2f'), horizontalalignment="center", color="black")
     - Why this is improvable: the code iterates cell-by-cell to place text. While matplotlib doesn't provide a fully vectorized text-annotation call, one can build a single array of formatted strings and use a compact loop over indices; however this is a visualization task (small matrices), and the performance gain is minimal.
     - Suggested alternative (same result, clearer):

       text_array = np.vectorize(lambda v: format(v, '.2f'))(average_cm)
       for (i, j), txt in np.ndenumerate(text_array):
           plt.text(j, i, txt, ha='center', color='black')

       trainLabels['path'] = [os.path.join(base_image_dir, '{}.jpeg'.format(x)) for x in trainLabels['image']]
       trainLabels['exists'] = [os.path.exists(p) for p in trainLabels['path']]  # Filter out missing images
     - Why this is improvable: constructing a pandas Series of file paths can be done with vectorized string operations which are implemented in C and faster than Python-level list comprehensions.
     - Suggested vectorized replacement (exact same result):
       trainLabels['path'] = base_image_dir + '/' + trainLabels['image'].astype(str) + '.jpeg'
       # There is no fully vectorized os.path.exists in pandas, but you can still avoid a python list comprehension by using Series.map (which is clearer):
       trainLabels['exists'] = trainLabels['path'].map(lambda p: os.path.exists(p))
       # If you prefer a pure numpy approach (may be faster for many entries):
       import numpy as np
       exists_arr = np.fromiter((os.path.exists(p) for p in trainLabels['path']), dtype=bool, count=len(trainLabels))
       trainLabels['exists'] = exists_arr
     - Note: the first line replacement uses pandas vectorized string concatenation; the exists check must ultimately call OS per-path, but using Series.map or numpy.fromiter is clearer and avoids creating an intermediate Python list.

2) Streaming nested loops over tf.data Dataset to pick one example per class (can be implemented via array/mask ops after materializing batches)
   - File: [/workspace/repo/cnn-based-detection-of-diabetic-retinopathy/cnn-based-detection-of-diabetic-retinopathy.py:164-179]
     - Code excerpt (lines 165-178):
       def get_images_by_label(dataset, num_classes=5):
           images = [None] * num_classes
           labels = [None] * num_classes
           label_counts = {i: 0 for i in range(num_classes)}

           for image_batch, label_batch in dataset:
               for img, lbl in zip(image_batch, label_batch):
                   label = int(lbl)
                   if label_counts[label] == 0:
                       images[label] = img
                       labels[label] = lbl
                       label_counts[label] += 1
                   if sum(label_counts.values()) == num_classes:
                       return np.array(images), np.array(labels)
           return np.array(images), np.array(labels)
     - Why this is improvable: the nested Python loops iterate per-sample while the same outcome (one sample per class) can be produced by materializing the dataset into arrays and then using numpy boolean indexing/argmax to pick first occurrences per class. That replacement moves the per-sample work into vectorized numpy operations.
     - Suggested vectorized approach (conceptual replacement):
       # materialize dataset into arrays (one-time loop to collect batches, unavoidable when using tf.data)
       imgs = []
       lbls = []
       for image_batch, label_batch in dataset:
           imgs.append(image_batch.numpy())
           lbls.append(label_batch.numpy())
       imgs = np.concatenate(imgs, axis=0)
       lbls = np.concatenate(lbls, axis=0)

       # vectorized selection of first instance per class
       images_out = np.empty((num_classes,)+imgs.shape[1:], dtype=imgs.dtype)
       labels_out = np.empty((num_classes,), dtype=lbls.dtype)
       for c in range(num_classes):
           mask = (lbls == c)
           idx = np.argmax(mask)  # returns first True; ensure class exists
           images_out[c] = imgs[idx]
           labels_out[c] = lbls[idx]
       # Note: the final small loop over classes (num_classes typically small) is negligible compared to per-sample loops.
     - Explanation: the initial collection of all batches must iterate once over dataset; after that, the heavy, per-sample selection is performed by numpy masks and argmax/boolean indexing (vectorized), avoiding nested per-sample Python loops.

3) Confusion-matrix text annotation uses double loop over matrix entries (visualization; can be vectorized but not performance-critical)
   - File: [/workspace/repo/cnn-based-detection-of-diabetic-retinopathy/cnn-based-detection-of-diabetic-retinopathy.py:467-476]
     - Code excerpt (lines 475-476):
       for i, j in itertools.product(range(average_cm.shape[0]), range(average_cm.shape[1])):
           plt.text(j, i, format(average_cm[i, j], '.2f'), horizontalalignment="center", color="black")
     - Why this is improvable: the code iterates cell-by-cell to place text. While matplotlib doesn't provide a fully vectorized text-annotation call, one can build a single array of formatted strings and use a compact loop over indices; however this is a visualization task (small matrices), and the performance gain is minimal.

       text_array = np.vectorize(lambda v: format(v, '.2f'))(average_cm)

VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The notebook mixes oversampled training rows and the original validation rows into a single DataFrame and then calls split_by_idx with an off-by-one range that includes at least one index from the (oversampled) training block into the validation indices. Because oversampling uses sampling with replacement, this can (and very likely will) produce duplicate rows for the same image in train_df; with the incorrect split indices those duplicated images can remain elsewhere in the train block while one copy is assigned to validation — i.e. the same image can appear in both train and validation sets (data leakage). Model-selection steps (lr_find, fit_one_cycle) use the validation set, so those tuning steps may be influenced by leaked examples.

EVIDENCE:
- Oversampling function which uses sampling with replacement: [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling.py:135-140] (defines balance_data which calls x.sample(class_size, replace=True)).
- Train/validation split (no stratify argument) and comment: [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling.py:146-147].
- Oversampling applied to train_df, then concatenation with val_df to form combined DataFrame (training portion first, validation portion appended): [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling.py:166-174]. This creates a DataFrame whose first N rows are the oversampled training set (containing duplicates) and whose last M rows are validation.
- The split indices passed to fastai are range(len(train_df)-1, len(df)) which incorrectly includes the last index of the training block (off-by-one). See: [/workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling.py:203-206]. Because train_df contains duplicates from oversampling, including even one train-index in the validation index list can lead to the same image appearing both in the training set (other duplicate rows) and in validation — i.e. leakage.

Why this matters: the code performs hyperparameter/learning-rate selection and training using the fastai validation set (lr_find(), fit_one_cycle(), etc.). If validation contains examples that are also present in training due to duplication/leakage, reported validation metrics and any hyperparameter choices will be optimistically biased.

Suggested fixes (not required to pass):
- Change split_by_idx(range(len(train_df)-1, len(df))) to split_by_idx(range(len(train_df), len(df))) so the validation indices correspond exactly to the appended val_df rows.
- Alternatively, avoid concatenating and instead build the ImageItemList separately using .from_df on train_df and val_df (or use .split_by_idxs with explicit indices), or perform oversampling after performing the fastai split (i.e. operate on the DataBunch/train_ds only).

Because the repository contains this off-by-one split plus oversampling-with-replacement, I conclude the test fails.

That includes the last row of the oversampled training block in the validation split, so the class-imbalance handling leaks into validation data.
EVIDENCE: 
1) Oversampling implemented on the training split (extracted snippet): [/evidence/artifacts/oversampling_and_split.py:1-11] shows the balance_data(...) function and the call to oversample train_df.
2) The concatenation of oversampled train_df with val_df is shown here: [/evidence/artifacts/oversampling_and_split.py:13-16]. The notebook comment even states: "beginning of this dataframe is the oversampled training set, end is the validation set".
3) The dataset split that assigns validation indices is here: [/evidence/artifacts/oversampling_and_split.py:18-23], specifically the line: .split_by_idx(range(len(train_df)-1,len(df))) which uses len(train_df)-1 as the first validation index (an off-by-one). This will include the final row of the oversampled training block into the validation set.
4) Original source: the code above is taken from the notebook at /workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling.ipynb (cells creating train/val, oversampling, concat, and ImageItemList.split_by_idx).

Because validation receives at least one oversampled (training) example due to the off-by-one in split indices, the repository does not guarantee that class-imbalance handling applies only to training data. If you want I can: (a) produce a small patch to fix the off-by-one to range(len(train_df), len(df)); (b) run a quick test that prints the indices/classes assigned to train/val to empirically demonstrate the leak.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The notebook's reported metrics are not computed using the splits and splitting procedure claimed in the text. Specifically: (1) the code comment says an 80%/20% split "with stratification" but the train_test_split() call omits the stratify argument, so stratified splitting was not performed; (2) the validation indices passed to fastai (.split_by_idx(range(...))) are off-by-one and will include one extra row from the (oversampled) training block in the validation set, so the actual train/validation sizes do not match the stated 80/20 partition. The Cohen quadratic kappa metric itself is implemented as claimed (sklearn cohen_kappa_score with weights='quadratic' on argmax predictions), so the metric definition is correct, but the split errors make the reported metric values unreliable relative to the claims.
EVIDENCE:
- Non-stratified train/test split claimed but not implemented: [/workspace/repo/diabetic_retinopathy_script.py.py:146-147] shows the call and the comment: "train_df, val_df = train_test_split(df,test_size=0.2) # Here we will perform an 80%/20% split of the dataset, with stratification to keep similar distribution in validation set" — the code does not pass stratify=..., so stratification did not occur.
- Off-by-one in constructing fastai split indices: [/workspace/repo/diabetic_retinopathy_script.py.py:203-206] shows
  "src = (ImageItemList.from_df(df=df,path='./',cols='path') #get dataset from dataset
         .split_by_idx(range(len(train_df)-1,len(df))) #Splitting the dataset
         .label_from_df(cols='level') #obtain labels from the level column
       )"
  Using range(len(train_df)-1, len(df)) produces validation indices starting at len(train_df)-1 (inclusive) up to len(df)-1; this yields (len(val_df) + 1) validation indices — one more than the intended val_df size — and therefore moves one sample from the intended training block into validation, breaking the stated 80/20 split.
- Quadratic kappa implementation (matches claimed definition): [/workspace/repo/diabetic_retinopathy_script.py.py:236-238] shows
  "from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score
   def quadratic_kappa(y_hat, y):
       return torch.tensor(cohen_kappa_score(torch.argmax(y_hat,1), y, weights='quadratic'),device='cuda:0')"
  This uses sklearn's cohen_kappa_score with weights='quadratic' on the argmax predictions, which corresponds to Cohen's quadratic weighted kappa as claimed.

Additional notes (for reproducibility / suggested fix):
- To get the claimed behavior, change the train_test_split call to include stratify=df['level'] (or stratify=df.level) when splitting, e.g. train_df, val_df = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.2, stratify=df['level']).
- Fix the split_by_idx call to use range(len(train_df), len(df)) (start at len(train_df), not len(train_df)-1) so the validation indices are exactly the intended val_df rows.

Because the data-splitting (which determines which examples are used for training vs validation) is implemented incorrectly relative to the claims, the repository FAILs the test that "Reported metrics use the correct split(s) and the exact definitions claimed."

metadata.reason_text: The notebook's reported metrics are not computed using the splits and splitting procedure claimed in the text. Specifically: (1) the code comment says an 80%/20% split "with stratification" but the train_test_split() call omits the stratify argument, so stratified splitting was not performed; (2) the validation indices passed to fastai (.split_by_idx(range(...))) are off-by-one and will include one extra row from the (oversampled) training block in the validation set, so the actual train/validation sizes do not match the stated 80/20 partition. The Cohen quadratic kappa metric itself is implemented as claimed (sklearn cohen_kappa_score with weights='quadratic' on argmax predictions), so the metric definition is correct, but the split errors make the reported metric values unreliable relative to the claims.
metadata.evidence_text:
- Non-stratified train/test split claimed but not implemented: [/workspace/repo/diabetic_retinopathy_script.py.py:146-147] shows the call and the comment: "train_df, val_df = train_test_split(df,test_size=0.2) # Here we will perform an 80%/20% split of the dataset, with stratification to keep similar distribution in validation set" — the code does not pass stratify=..., so stratification did not occur.
- Off-by-one in constructing fastai split indices: [/workspace/repo/diabetic_retinopathy_script.py.py:203-206] shows
  "src = (ImageItemList.from_df(df=df,path='./',cols='path') #get dataset from dataset
         .split_by_idx(range(len(train_df)-1,len(df))) #Splitting the dataset
         .label_from_df(cols='level') #obtain labels from the level column
       )"
  Using range(len(train_df)-1, len(df)) produces validation indices starting at len(train_df)-1 (inclusive) up to len(df)-1; this yields (len(val_df) + 1) validation indices — one more than the intended val_df size — and therefore moves one sample from the intended training block into validation, breaking the stated 80/20 split.
- Quadratic kappa implementation (matches claimed definition): [/workspace/repo/diabetic_retinopathy_script.py.py:236-238] shows
  "from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score
   def quadratic_kappa(y_hat, y):

  This uses sklearn's cohen_kappa_score with weights='quadratic' on the argmax predictions, which corresponds to Cohen's quadratic weighted kappa as claimed.

- To get the claimed behavior, change the train_test_split call to include stratify=df['level'] (or stratify=df.level) when splitting, e.g. train_df, val_df = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.2, stratify=df['level']).
- Fix the split_by_idx call to use range(len(train_df), len(df)) (start at len(train_df), not len(train_df)-1) so the validation indices are exactly the intended val_df rows.

tests.description:
VERDICT: FAIL
REASON: The repository contains an explicit metric implementation that forces CPU↔GPU transfers and assumes a specific device. quadratic_kappa builds a sklearn metric from torch tensors and then wraps the scalar back into a torch.tensor pinned to 'cuda:0' — this mixes CPU-only (sklearn) and GPU tensors and will cause implicit device transfers or runtime errors when the model/device differs. There is no consistent dtype policy (no fp16/bf16 setup) anywhere in the code.
EVIDENCE: 
- Metric mixes sklearn (CPU) and GPU tensors: [/workspace/repo/diabetic_notebook_converted.py:108-112] shows the problematic code:
  - line 109: from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score
  - line 110-111: def quadratic_kappa(y_hat, y):
                   return torch.tensor(cohen_kappa_score(torch.argmax(y_hat,1), y, weights='quadratic'),device='cuda:0')
  This calls sklearn.cohe n_kappa_score on torch tensors (which expects CPU/NumPy arrays) and then constructs a torch.tensor explicitly on device='cuda:0', implying an implicit CPU<->GPU transfer and a hard dependency on CUDA device index 0.
- Data and model creation (no explicit device/dtype orchestration): [/workspace/repo/diabetic_notebook_converted.py:96-99] shows DataBunch creation via fastai (no dtype control), and [/workspace/repo/diabetic_notebook_converted.py:115] shows create_cnn used to make the model. There is no code that consistently moves both model and inputs to a single device or configures a dtype policy (fp32/fp16/bf16) for training.
- The notebook also queries CUDA availability but does not use the result to conditionally set device in the metric: [/workspace/repo/diabetic_notebook_converted.py:31-33].

Because of the explicit device hardcoding and the mixing of sklearn (CPU) with GPU tensors, the repository fails the requirement that model and inputs are consistently moved to one device with no implicit CPU↔GPU transfers; dtype policy is also not applied consistently.

Files cited exist in the repository as converted from the notebook: /workspace/repo/diabetic_notebook_converted.py (derived from the original notebook at /workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling.ipynb).

  - line 109: from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score
  - line 110-111: def quadratic_kappa(y_hat, y):
                   return torch.tensor(cohen_kappa_score(torch.argmax(y_hat,1), y, weights='quadratic'),device='cuda:0')
  This calls sklearn.cohe n_kappa_score on torch tensors (which expects CPU/NumPy arrays) and then constructs a torch.tensor explicitly on device='cuda:0', implying an implicit CPU<->GPU transfer and a hard dependency on CUDA device index 0.
- Data and model creation (no explicit device/dtype orchestration): [/workspace/repo/diabetic_notebook_converted.py:96-99] shows DataBunch creation via fastai (no dtype control), and [/workspace/repo/diabetic_notebook_converted.py:115] shows create_cnn used to make the model. There is no code that consistently moves both model and inputs to a single device or configures a dtype policy (fp32/fp16/bf16) for training.
- The notebook also queries CUDA availability but does not use the result to conditionally set device in the metric: [/workspace/repo/diabetic_notebook_converted.py:31-33].

Because of the explicit device hardcoding and the mixing of sklearn (CPU) with GPU tensors, the repository fails the requirement that model and inputs are consistently moved to one device with no implicit CPU↔GPU transfers; dtype policy is also not applied consistently.

Files cited exist in the repository as converted from the notebook: /workspace/repo/diabetic_notebook_converted.py (derived from the original notebook at /workspace/repo/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling/diabetic-retinopathy-with-resnet50-oversampling.ipynb).
